chapters.n: Paul, Silas, and Timothy write again to the Thessalonians, probably only a few months after the first letter, to correct confusion about Christ’s coming.
The familiar greeting of grace and peace from the Father and the Son.
Paul feels obligated to thank God, because their faith is growing dramatically and their love for one another keeps increasing — an answer to his earlier prayer.
Paul even brags about them to other branches because they endure persecution with patience and faith.
Their faithful endurance is evidence that God’s judgment is just: they are being made worthy of God’s kingdom, the very cause for which they suffer.
God is just: He will repay with trouble those who trouble His people.
And He will give relief and rest to the persecuted Saints when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with His mighty angels.
He will come in blazing fire, bringing justice on those who refuse to know God and reject the gospel.

f.g: Just punishment, rendering justice — not personal spite.

chapters.n: Their penalty will be separation from the Lord’s presence and glory. Scripture describes being cut off from God as the deepest form of punishment.

f.w: everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord

chapters.n: On that day Christ will be glorified in His Saints and marveled at by all who believed — including the Thessalonians, who accepted the apostles’ testimony.
So Paul prays that God will make them worthy of their calling and, by His power, bring every good desire and act of faith to completion.
Then Christ’s name will be honored in them, and they in Him — all by the grace of God and Christ. Glory flows both ways between the Lord and His disciples.

f.w: glorified in you, and ye in him

chapters.n: Paul now addresses the main issue: the Lord’s coming and our being gathered to Him.
Don’t be quickly shaken or alarmed by any claim — whether a supposed spiritual revelation, a report, or a forged letter in Paul’s name — saying the Day of the Lord has already arrived.

f.g: A forged letter claiming to be Paul’s.

chapters.n: Don’t be fooled: that day won’t come until a great rebellion — a falling away — happens first, and the “man of sin,” the son of perdition, is revealed. Latter-day Saints see this as foretelling the Great Apostasy before the Restoration.
This figure opposes God and exalts himself above everything worshipped, even seating himself in God’s temple and claiming to be God — a picture of Satan’s ambition to usurp God’s place.

f.w: sitteth in the temple of God

chapters.n: Paul reminds them that he taught them these things in person. His letters assume earlier oral teaching we don’t fully have.
They know what is holding this evil back so it will be revealed only at its proper time.

The secret power of lawlessness is already at work, but it is being held in check until the restraint is removed. The JST reads that Satan now works and “Christ suffereth him to work, until the time is fulfilled.”
Then the lawless one will be revealed — and the Lord will destroy him with the breath of His mouth and the splendor of His coming.
His arrival will be powered by Satan, with counterfeit miracles, signs, and false wonders.
He will use every kind of evil deception on those who are perishing — because they refused to love the truth that could save them.
Because they reject truth, God allows them to be overtaken by a powerful delusion so they believe falsehood. People who turn from light lose the ability to see.

f.g: A working of error; God permits the consequence of rejecting truth.

chapters.n: So all who rejected truth and enjoyed wickedness will be condemned.
By contrast, Paul gives thanks for the Thessalonians, loved by the Lord and chosen by God for salvation through the Spirit’s sanctifying work and their belief in the truth.
God called them through the gospel Paul preached, so they can share in the glory of the Lord Jesus Christ.

f.w: the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ

chapters.n: So stand firm and hold on to the teachings passed on to you — in person or by letter.

f.g: Teachings handed down — here the apostles’ authorized teaching.

chapters.n: Paul prays that the Lord Jesus and the Father — who loved us and gave eternal encouragement and good hope through grace —
will comfort their hearts and strengthen them in every good thing they say and do.
Paul asks for prayers that the Lord’s message will spread rapidly and be honored elsewhere, as it was among them.
Pray also that we will be rescued from perverse and evil people — for not everyone has faith.
But the Lord is faithful; He will strengthen you and protect you from the evil one.
Paul is confident in the Lord that they are following and will continue to follow his instructions.
May the Lord guide your hearts into God’s love and into the patient endurance that Christ gives.

f.g: Or “the steadfastness of Christ” — endurance like His.

chapters.n: With Christ’s authority Paul commands them to keep away from any member who lives idly and ignores the teachings received from the apostles.

f.g: Lives out of line — here especially refusing to work.

chapters.n: They know they should imitate Paul’s example; he was never idle while among them.
He didn’t eat anyone’s food without paying. He worked hard, day and night, so he wouldn’t burden anyone.
Paul had the right to be supported as an apostle, but he chose to work so he could model the pattern for them.
His rule while among them: whoever refuses to work shouldn’t eat. This targets the unwilling, not those unable to work.
Paul has heard that some are idle — not busy working, but busybodies meddling in others’ affairs.

f.g: Wordplay in Greek: not busy at work but busy in others’ business.

chapters.n: He commands such people, in the Lord Jesus, to settle down, work quietly, and earn their own living.
To the rest he says: never tire of doing what is right.

f.w: be not weary in well doing

chapters.n: If anyone ignores this letter’s instructions, take note of him and don’t associate closely with him, so he may feel ashamed and change.
But don’t treat him as an enemy; warn him as a brother. The goal of discipline is restoring, not rejecting.
Paul prays that the Lord of peace Himself will give them peace at all times and in every way.
Paul writes the closing in his own handwriting — the mark of authenticity in all his letters, guarding against forgeries like the one mentioned in 2:2.
He ends with Christ’s grace upon everyone.
